Auth.js v5 fail-open trigger: server-configuration error in application logs AIExploitation High
Hunts for the Auth.js (next-auth v5) server-side configuration error that, per GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3, silently flips existence-based auth checks (`!!auth` / `if(req.auth)`) to always-true — treating every unauthenticated visitor as logged in. Fires when the app emits `[auth][error]` markers such as `InvalidEndpoints` or the 'problem with the server configuration' message, which is the exact precondition for the fail-open authorization bypass. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact log strings — the `[auth][error]` prefix plus the `InvalidEndpoints` / 'problem with the server configuration' / unset `AUTH_SECRET` conditions the advisory names as triggers for the truthy error-object that makes `!!auth` permanently true. These strings are emitted only on genuine Auth.js config failure, giving very low FP and directly flagging the window during which existence-based route protection is bypassed.
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Transient error during a rolling deploy before env vars (AUTH_SECRET / provider issuer) propagate to all instances
  • Developer or CI intentionally exercising a broken provider config in a dev/staging environment shipping to the same index
  • A monitoring/health-check tool echoing the error message back in its own log output
  • A previous, already-remediated misconfiguration whose log lines are still inside the search window
  • Unrelated component quoting the literal 'problem with the server configuration' phrase in an error handler
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/service that emitted the marker and confirm the app actually uses existence-based checks (`!!auth` / `if(req.auth)`) and is internet-facing; verify whether AUTH_SECRET or the provider issuer/authorization endpoint is genuinely missing. 2) Contain: treat as a production auth outage — roll back the offending deploy or restore the missing env var, or take the affected routes offline until auth is confirmed working; do not leave protected routes reachable while the error persists. 3) Hunt: review HTTP/access logs for the window between first and last `[auth][error]` for unauthenticated access to protected paths, upgrade next-auth to the patched beta, and change checks to `!!req.auth?.user` plus explicit role checks.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("InvalidEndpoints", "There was a problem with the server configuration", "MissingSecret", "AUTH_SECRET")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog "[auth][error]" AND ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "There was a problem with the server configuration" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET")
# log group: point at your Next.js / Auth.js app log group (e.g. /aws/lambda/<ssr-fn> or Amplify SSR compute log group)
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @message like /\[auth\]\[error\]/
      and @message like /InvalidEndpoints|There was a problem with the server configuration|MissingSecret|AUTH_SECRET/
| sort @timestamp desc
APPLICATION
index=* ("[auth][error]") ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "There was a problem with the server configuration" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET")
| stats count AS hits, min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS lastSeen, values(host) AS hosts, values(source) AS sources BY sourcetype
| sort - lastSeen

CL-STA-1114 Zimbra espionage C2 / exfiltration channel contact (9 domains + 9 IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint, proxy, or firewall traffic to the hard-coded command-and-control infrastructure the injected Zimbra JavaScript payload uses to exfiltrate CSRF tokens, credentials, 2FA scratch codes and 90 days of mail/search history. Article-specific because it pins the exact nine domains and nine IPs Unit 42 attributed to CL-STA-1114. Rationale: Anchored on the nine C2 domains and nine C2 IPs Unit 42 explicitly attributes to CL-STA-1114; several domains (zimbrastat, mailnalysis, zmailanalytics, synacorzimbra) impersonate Zimbra/Synacor analytics services, so any resolution/connection is high-fidelity. IPs cover the NetworkConnectIP4 side the DnsRequest lead query omits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-apt28-military-hackers-exploit-zimbra-flaw-in-ukrainian-govt-attacks/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / TI-platform sandbox detonating the same IOCs from a corporate egress IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively resolving IOC domains for feed validation
  • A parked/sinkholed IOC domain re-registered by a legitimate service after the 35-day average C2 lifetime expired
  • DNS resolver logging a passive-DNS crawler rather than a real client beacon
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal src host/user and the initiating process (browser vs. server); confirm whether the host is a Zimbra webmail user and pull the surrounding 5 min of proxy/DNS for the same session. 2) Contain: block all nine domains and nine IPs at DNS/firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and force-reset the affected user's mailbox password + revoke sessions and 2FA scratch codes (the payload steals these). 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs for the remaining IOCs org-wide, review Zimbra Classic UI access logs for the triggering email, and check for exfil volume spikes to the C2 over the connection window.

Inbound HTML-attachment / embedded-HTML Zimbra XSS lure (CVE-2025-66376 delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CL-STA-1114 initial-access vector: inbound emails carrying an HTML attachment (or embedded HTML) with news-headline lures that trigger the zero-click Zimbra Classic UI XSS via unsanitized CSS @import directives. Also fires high-confidence when a delivered message references one of the campaign's C2 domains. Rationale: Unit 42 states initial access is a phishing email with an HTML attachment or embedded HTML using news-headline lures; corroboration (SentinelOne/Tenable) pins the exploit to CSS @import in HTML mail, so HTML attachments are THE delivery vector. The C2-domain URL clause (Reason=C2-domain-in-message) is a named-IOC alerting-grade match; the HTML-attachment clause is the broader hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2025-66376 • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-ghostmail-zimbra-xss-russian-apt-ukraine/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1203 T1059.007 T1539
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing newsletters and receipts delivered as .html/.htm attachments
  • DocuSign / e-signature and HR portals that send HTML form attachments
  • Automated report exports (BI dashboards, monitoring alerts) mailed as HTML files
  • Internal newsletters relayed inbound via a distribution list
  • Legitimate email-analytics vendors whose tracking domains superficially resemble the C2 naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the HTML attachment/body in a sandbox and grep for CSS @import, base64 blobs, or an invisible <svg onload=...> that decodes script — the CVE-2025-66376 signature; confirm the recipient uses Zimbra Classic UI. 2) Contain: quarantine/purge the message from all recipient mailboxes (soft-delete), block the sender and any embedded domains, and confirm ZCS is patched to 10.0.18 / 10.1.13. 3) Hunt: pivot on sender infrastructure and subject/lure across the tenant, and correlate any opener with UC-1 C2 egress within the following minutes to catch successful exfiltration.

Unpatched Zimbra Collaboration Suite exposed to CVE-2025-66376 AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces hosts running Zimbra Collaboration Suite versions vulnerable to the CVE-2025-66376 Classic UI stored-XSS that CL-STA-1114 weaponizes for zero-click JS injection, so exposure can be remediated (patch to 10.0.18 / 10.1.13) before exploitation. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE (CVE-2025-66376) named in the article and confirmed by CISA KEV/Tenable/SentinelOne, with corroborated fixed versions ZCS 10.0.18 and 10.1.13; a TVM lookup on that CveId cleanly enumerates exposed Zimbra hosts without version-string parsing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2025-66376 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1203
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host patched to 10.0.18/10.1.13 but not yet rescanned by TVM (stale inventory)
  • Zimbra appliance running on Linux not fully onboarded to MDE, causing under-reporting rather than false positives
  • Test/lab ZCS instance flagged but not internet-facing or not processing external mail
  • Compensating control (WAF/mail-sanitizer stripping CSS @import) already mitigating despite version match
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged ZCS version is below 10.0.18 (v10) or 10.1.13 (v10.1) and whether the Classic UI is enabled and internet-reachable. 2) Contain: prioritize patching to the fixed version; as an interim control, disable Classic UI or deploy the Zimbra mitigation and enforce mail-body CSS/HTML sanitization at the gateway. 3) Hunt: on any still-vulnerable host, retro-hunt UC-1 C2 IOCs and UC-2 inbound HTML lures across the exposure window to determine whether it was already exploited.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| order by files desc

Claude Cowork Flaw Could Let AI Agent Escape Its VM and Access Mac Files

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 14 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a sandbox escape vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude Cowork that makes it possible to break out of the confines of a Linux virtual machine (VM) within which the agent runs to read or write files anywhere on the Mac. Accomplish AI, which shared details of the vulnerability with The Hacker News ahead of publication, said about 500,000 macOS users running

CVEsCVE-2026-46331
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] pedit COW (CVE-2026-46331) exploitation via tc act_pedit inside Claude Cowork guest VM · [LLM] Unprivileged user+network namespace creation chained to net/sched exploit (SharedRoot prereq) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Guest process accessing host filesystem via /mnt/.virtiofs-root (SharedRoot host escape) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
pedit COW (CVE-2026-46331) exploitation via tc act_pedit inside Claude Cowork guest VM AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core privilege-escalation primitive of the SharedRoot Cowork sandbox escape: an unprivileged Linux process invoking the traffic-control act_pedit action (`tc ... action pedit`), autoloading the act_pedit module, or running the public packet_edit_meme PoC to trigger CVE-2026-46331 and obtain guest-root. This is article-specific because a normal Cowork agent session has no legitimate reason to touch the net/sched packet-editor path. Rationale: Uses the article's named exploit primitive (act_pedit / tc packet-editor) plus the second-source-confirmed PoC name packet_edit_meme and module string act_pedit from the CVE-2026-46331 write-ups; the net/sched pedit path has no benign use inside a Cowork agent VM. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://tuxcare.com/blog/pedit-cow-cve/ • https://canonical.com/blog/pedit-cow-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available • https://cyberpress.org/packet_edit_meme-linux-kernel-flaw/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network/QoS engineers legitimately configuring tc pedit rules on Linux routers or shaping hosts
  • CI/CD or container-networking tooling (CNI plugins) that programs tc actions
  • Security researchers running the PoC in an isolated lab VM
  • Kernel module diagnostics loading net/sched modules during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tc-cni","cni","kubelet","dockerd","containerd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a Claude Cowork guest VM (Apple Virtualization) or a general Linux endpoint; a Cowork agent session invoking tc/act_pedit is never legitimate — capture the full command line, UID and parent process. 2) Contain: terminate the Cowork local session, kill the offending process tree, and isolate the host; rotate any SSH keys / cloud credentials stored under the logged-in Mac user account. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for prior unprivileged user+network namespace creation (unshare) and for any subsequent access to /mnt/.virtiofs-root; verify guest kernel is patched to a build past Linux v7.1-rc7 / vendor backport and that unprivileged user namespaces are disabled.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "tc" and ProcessCommandLine has "pedit")
   or (FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod") and ProcessCommandLine has "act_pedit")
   or FileName =~ "packet_edit_meme"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "tc" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "pedit")
   or (ActingProcessName has_any ("modprobe","insmod","kmod") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "act_pedit")
   or ActingProcessName has "packet_edit_meme"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unprivileged user+network namespace creation chained to net/sched exploit (SharedRoot prereq) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the two-step prerequisite the SharedRoot escape needs: an unprivileged process creating a user AND network namespace (via unshare) to gain CAP_NET_ADMIN, followed within minutes on the same host/user by a tc act_pedit / module-load / packet_edit_meme invocation. The namespaces are not the exploit but make the normally-privileged act_pedit path reachable, so the temporal pairing is high-fidelity. Rationale: Encodes the article's stated prerequisite — 'creating user and network namespaces gives the session CAP_NET_ADMIN … that capability provides access to the vulnerable tc/act_pedit path' — as a 5-minute temporal join, turning two individually-noisy events into an article-specific chain. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/claude-cowork-flaw-could-let-ai-agent.html • https://tuxcare.com/blog/pedit-cow-cve/
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rootless container runtimes (Podman, Docker rootless, bubblewrap) that unshare user+net namespaces then program tc
  • Kubernetes CNI setup on a node that creates netns and applies tc shaping close in time
  • Sandboxing tools (firejail, nsjail) used by developers
  • Network test harnesses spinning up isolated namespaces for tc experiments
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and DeviceName !has "k8s" and NsCmd !has "firejail"
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host, order the unshare and tc/act_pedit events and confirm same UID and a sub-5-minute gap; a Cowork VM session or interactive user with no container/CNI role is high-suspicion. 2) Contain: suspend the session, freeze the VM for forensics, and isolate the host from file shares before rotating host-user secrets. 3) Hunt: check whether unprivileged user namespaces are enabled (kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone), look for follow-on writes/reads under /mnt/.virtiofs-root, and confirm guest kernel patch level against CVE-2026-46331 (fixed v7.1-rc7).

| where (ProcessCommandLine has "--net"  or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-[a-z]*n")
| project NsTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, NsCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "tc" and ProcessCommandLine has "pedit")
   or (FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod") and ProcessCommandLine has "act_pedit")

| where Timestamp between (NsTime .. NsTime + 5m)
| project NsTime, ExploitTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, NsCmd, ExploitCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FileName
| order by ExploitTime desc
let ns = ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "unshare"
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--user" or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-[a-z]*u")
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--net"  or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-[a-z]*n")
| project NsTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, NsCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "tc" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "pedit")
   or (ActingProcessName has_any ("modprobe","insmod") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "act_pedit")
   or ActingProcessName has "packet_edit_meme"
| join kind=inner ns on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (NsTime .. NsTime + 5m)

| order by ExploitTime desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, NsCmd, CommandLine], function=count())

Guest process accessing host filesystem via /mnt/.virtiofs-root (SharedRoot host escape) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual sandbox escape and credential theft: any process inside the Claude Cowork guest VM (other than the coworkd mount daemon) reading or writing the host Mac's root filesystem exposed read-write at /mnt/.virtiofs-root. This is the single most article-specific IOC — that exact mount path is the read-write bridge to the host, so agent/session access to it (e.g. cat/cp/tar of SSH keys or cloud credentials) is definitive. Rationale: Anchors on the literal escape path /mnt/.virtiofs-root named in the article (host '/' mounted read-write, visible only to guest-root) and excludes the legitimate coworkd mount daemon, so any remaining hit is the escape itself; secret-path enrichment prioritises SSH-key/cloud-credential theft the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/claude-cowork-flaw-could-let-ai-agent.html • https://gbhackers.com/claude-cowork-sandbox-flaw/ • https://threat-modeling.com/anthropic-claude-cowork-sandbox-escape-root-access/
ATT&CKT1611 T1552.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Anthropic coworkd/mount tooling legitimately establishing or tearing down the virtiofs share (excluded)
  • Support/diagnostic scripts explicitly inspecting the mount during vendor troubleshooting
  • A user intentionally scripting file operations against the connected folder if the tool exposes that path
  • Backup or AV agents scanning mounted paths inside the VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "anthropic-support" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process and UID referencing /mnt/.virtiofs-root and whether it touched .ssh, .aws, gcloud, or .kube paths (TouchesSecrets=true) — read/copy of those = confirmed host credential theft. 2) Contain: kill the process, terminate the Cowork local session, snapshot then destroy the guest VM, and immediately rotate the logged-in Mac user's SSH keys and all cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure/Kube) credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate backward to the pedit COW exploit (UC1) and namespace prereq (UC2) on the same host, and forward to any outbound egress or new sessions authenticating with the stolen keys; advise moving affected users to Cowork cloud execution which does not expose the host mount.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/mnt/.virtiofs-root"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("coworkd","mount","mount.virtiofs") and FileName !in~ ("coworkd","mount","mount.virtiofs")
| extend TouchesSecrets = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/.ssh/","/.aws/","id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","/.config/gcloud","/.kube/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, TouchesSecrets,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TouchesSecrets desc, Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/mnt/.virtiofs-root"
| where ActingProcessName !has "coworkd" and ActingProcessName !has "mount"
| extend TouchesSecrets = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/.ssh/","/.aws/","id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","/.config/gcloud","/.kube/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TouchesSecrets, ParentProcessName
| order by TouchesSecrets desc, TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

Chaos Ransomware Uses msaRAT to Route C2 Traffic Through Headless Chrome and Edge

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 18 use cases 10 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group ran its command-and-control through the victim's own browser. Cisco Talos on Thursday detailed msaRAT, the Rust implant behind it, found on a compromised Windows machine ahead of the encryptor. The implant never opens an outbound connection of its own. Its process talks to 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. It starts Chrome or Edge in headless mode and drives the browser

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1219 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT MSI stager pulled by curl.exe from Chaos staging IP to C:\programdata · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] msaRAT command execution via cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c signature · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chaos Ransomware Uses msaRAT to Route C2 Traffic Through Headless Chrome and Edg
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Headless Chrome/Edge with CDP debugging launched by non-interactive parent (msaRAT C2) · [LLM] Headless browser beaconing to Chaos Cloudflare Worker / Twilio TURN relay (msaRAT WebRTC C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
msaRAT MSI stager pulled by curl.exe from Chaos staging IP to C:\programdata AIDelivery High
Hunts the msaRAT delivery step where curl.exe downloads a fake Windows-update MSI (update_ms.msi) from the Chaos staging host 172.86.126.18 over port 443 into C:\programdata. Anchored on the exact staging IP and payload filename Talos published, not on generic curl usage. Rationale: Uses two article-specific IOCs from the single documented delivery command: staging IP 172.86.126.18 and the payload filename update_ms.msi. Both are concrete strings from Talos; either match is high-fidelity because neither is a normal curl target. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually testing curl against an internal host that happens to share the IP octet pattern (unlikely — full IP match)
  • Software packaging engineer naming a legitimate MSI update_ms.msi (rare)
  • Security researcher replaying the Talos IOC in a sandbox
  • curl download-manager scripts pulling MSIs from an internal repo (won't match the exact IP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and parent process; confirm the destination is 172.86.126.18 and the output path is C:\programdata\update_ms.msi. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 172.86.126.18 at the egress firewall, and quarantine C:\programdata\update_ms.msi before msiexec runs it. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a subsequent msiexec execution of update_ms.msi and any chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --headless=new and --remote-debugging-port (msaRAT C2 stage).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "172.86.126.18" or ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "172.86.126.18" or CommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Headless Chrome/Edge with CDP debugging launched by non-interactive parent (msaRAT C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the msaRAT C2 stage: Chrome or Edge started with --headless=new and --remote-debugging-port by an installer/service/non-Explorer parent, which drives the browser over CDP to relay C2. This is the durable behavioural signal Talos flags, distinct from a user opening a browser window. Rationale: Anchored on the two exact launch flags Talos names (--headless=new + --remote-debugging-port) plus the non-interactive-parent constraint that separates malicious CDP abuse from a user's browser session. This is the 'signal that lasts' the article calls out because the technique, unlike the IP/domain, cannot be swapped. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD pipelines running Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium headless jobs (parent is node.exe/python.exe/dotnet.exe)
  • Synthetic monitoring / browser-test agents (Datadog, Catchpoint) launching headless Chrome
  • Server-side HTML-to-PDF or screenshot rendering services
  • Enterprise browser telemetry/health tooling spawning headless instances from a service
  • RPA bots automating web forms via a scheduled task
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe","dotnet.exe","java.exe","chromedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process — legitimate automation is parented by node.exe/python.exe/a CI runner, whereas msaRAT is parented by msiexec.exe, a service, or an unsigned in-memory host. Check the --user-data-dir path (msaRAT uses a fresh non-default profile). 2) Contain: if the parent is unexpected, isolate the host and suspend the headless browser process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate the browser PID with loopback traffic to the --remote-debugging-port and outbound connections to *.workers.dev / global.turn.twilio.com, and check for the earlier curl/update_ms.msi delivery.

| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless=new" and ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Headless browser beaconing to Chaos Cloudflare Worker / Twilio TURN relay (msaRAT WebRTC C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the outbound half of msaRAT's browser-relayed C2: a Chrome/Edge process resolving/connecting to the Chaos signaling Worker is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, or reaching Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) from a headless instance. Anchored on the exact Worker host Talos published plus the headless-browser context that separates it from ordinary WebRTC apps. Rationale: Uses the exact signaling Worker host is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev (a confirmed second-source IOC) as an alert, and pairs generic Twilio TURN egress with the --headless=new browser context so the behavioural clause survives IOC rotation. Confidence is Medium because Talos notes both network artifacts are trivially swappable. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/msarat-chrome-edge-browser-c2/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different, benign Cloudflare Workers app deployed under a similar subdomain (exact-host match avoids this)
  • Legitimate WebRTC/conferencing apps (Teams, Zoom, softphones) reaching Twilio TURN — filtered out by the headless-browser clause on the Twilio branch
  • Threat-intel/EDR products beaconing the IOC for enrichment
  • Security team detonating the sample in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host resolved is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and which process initiated it (expect a headless chrome.exe/msedge.exe). 2) Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block the Worker host and monitor global.turn.twilio.com egress from that host; do NOT org-wide block Twilio TURN (breaks legit WebRTC). 3) Hunt: pivot to the browser PID for the --remote-debugging-port loopback session, look for the update_ms.msi delivery and cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c command execution, and prepare for a possible Chaos encryptor stage.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where (RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev")
     or (RemoteUrl endswith "turn.twilio.com" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--headless=new")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT command execution via cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c signature AIExploitation High
Hunts msaRAT's command-dispatch primitive, which executes every received C2 command frame through the fixed invocation cmd.exe /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c <cmd>. The exact ordered flag string is an unusual automation signature that distinguishes implant-driven shell execution from normal cmd usage. Rationale: The contiguous flag string /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c is a verbatim msaRAT artifact from the Talos analysis; this precise flag ordering (extensions on, delayed-expansion off, skip-autorun, run-and-exit) is rarely emitted by legitimate software, making the substring match high-fidelity even without hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche installer or automation framework that hardcodes the same /e:ON /v:OFF /d /c flag combo (uncommon)
  • Custom RMM/orchestration agents wrapping shell commands with explicit cmd extension flags
  • Red-team tooling replicating msaRAT for detection validation
  • In-house scripts generated by a build system that pins delayed-expansion off
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full cmd.exe command line and its parent — msaRAT's parent is the in-memory Rust implant host (often a browser-adjacent or msiexec-spawned process), not a user shell. Review the child command being run. 2) Contain: isolate the host and suspend the implant host process tree; preserve memory for the Tokio/Rust DLL (exports RUN). 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for headless chrome/msedge with --remote-debugging-port, egress to the Worker/Twilio TURN infrastructure, and the update_ms.msi delivery; escalate as pre-ransomware activity given the Chaos linkage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "/e:ON /v:OFF /d /c"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine contains "/e:ON /v:OFF /d /c"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the fixed cmd.exe invocation string (/e:ON /v:OFF /d /c) that msaRAT uses to execute each incoming C2 command frame.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\cmd.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/e:ON /v:OFF /d /c'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\Cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE) @CommandLine:(*e\:ON* OR *e\:on*) @CommandLine:(*v\:OFF* OR *v\:off*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\cmd\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\/e:ON\s+\/v:OFF\s+\/d\s+\/c/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cmd.exe Processes.process="*/e:ON /v:OFF /d /c*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cmd.exe Processes.process="*/e:ON /v:OFF /d /c*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
