Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"

         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Nexus JadeProx Uses New TriBack Loader in Government and Healthcare Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 20 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An exposed Alibaba Cloud server has revealed a China-nexus operation that Group-IB tracks as JadeProx. The cluster has targeted government, healthcare, and education organizations across Asia and Latin America with a previously undocumented Windows loader called TriBack Loader. Group-IB found the server in mid-April 2026 in Alibaba Cloud's Singapore region; it was offline by the time the report

TriBack Loader DLL side-load: avk.dll/MpClient.dll/hostfxr.dll from user-writable dirs AIInstallation High
Hunts JadeProx's TriBack Loader triad where a legitimate signed vendor binary (G DATA's NOVupdate.exe, Microsoft's MpCopyAccelerator.exe) is dropped into a user-writable folder alongside a malicious replacement DLL and an encrypted .dat/.log payload. Detects the malicious avk.dll, MpClient.dll, or hostfxr.dll being image-loaded from AppData/Temp/Public/Startup/ProgramData rather than their legitimate Program Files homes. Rationale: Anchors on Sophos-confirmed signed hosts (NOVupdate.exe/MpCopyAccelerator.exe) plus the three malicious DLL names named by Group-IB (avk.dll, MpClient.dll, hostfxr.dll); the discriminator is the user-writable load path, since legit copies of these DLLs only ever load from Program Files\G DATA, Program Files\Windows Defender, or a dotnet host dir. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-claude-ai-website-delivers-new-beagle-windows-malware/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/standalone build of a G DATA product staged from a user Temp folder during troubleshooting
  • A .NET single-file app self-extracting hostfxr.dll into %TEMP% or %LOCALAPPDATA% on first run
  • Software packaged/repackaged by an admin that copies MpClient.dll into ProgramData for testing
  • Security-tool sandbox or detonation VM that stages vendor binaries in a working directory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\G DATA\", @"\Program Files\Windows Defender\", @"\Program Files\dotnet\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full folder listing of the load path — confirm a signed host EXE, a same-named .dat, or Windows.log sits beside the DLL; verify the DLL's Authenticode signature (malicious avk.dll/MpClient.dll are unsigned or mismatched). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the parent EXE hash, and quarantine the folder before the Startup entry re-runs it at logon. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same triad filenames, then pivot the host's outbound traffic to the UC4 domain/IP list to confirm AdaptixC2/Beagle beaconing.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("avk.dll","MpClient.dll","hostfxr.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("NOVupdate.exe","MpCopyAccelerator.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Startup\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

JadeProx Startup-folder persistence: side-load triad dropped by msiexec AIInstallation High
Detects the Claude-impersonation MSI (Claude.msi/GolddTV.msi) planting the TriBack side-load chain into the user's Startup folder past a UAC prompt. Fires when the signed host EXE, malicious DLL, or encrypted payload is created under \Start Menu\Programs\Startup\. Rationale: Combines the Sophos-named payload/host filenames with the article's explicit persistence mechanism (side-load chain placed in Windows Startup folder). A signed vendor EXE plus a .dat/.log companion appearing in a per-user Startup path is not a legitimate installer behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fake-claude-site-beagle-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit .lnk-based app auto-start creation (excluded here — we match EXE/DLL/.dat/.log, not .lnk)
  • Backup/sync agent restoring a user's Startup folder onto a rebuilt machine
  • In-house software that legitimately drops a vendor updater EXE into Startup
  • Roaming-profile replication copying Startup contents at logon
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".dat" or FileName endswith ".log"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess is msiexec.exe or an unsigned dropper and check whether all three triad members (host EXE + DLL + payload) landed together. 2) Contain: delete the Startup entries, isolate the host, and block the delivering MSI hash tenant-wide. 3) Hunt: search UrlClickEvents/DNS for claude-pro.com or the security-vendor lookalike domains that delivered the MSI, and check for the same triad on other endpoints of the affected user.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName in~ ("NOVupdate.exe","MpCopyAccelerator.exe","avk.dll","MpClient.dll","NOVupdate.exe.dat","Windows.log")
    or (FileName endswith ".dat" or FileName endswith ".log")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("NOVupdate.exe","MpCopyAccelerator.exe","avk.dll","MpClient.dll","NOVupdate.exe.dat","Windows.log")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

TriBack Loader staging artifacts: ~del.vbs.bat and nested _CL_###### folders AIInstallation High
Hunts the distinctive filesystem debris of the JadeProx side-load chain: the ~del.vbs.bat cleanup script and the nested _CL_###### staging folders it drops. These filenames are unique to this operation and change far less than the per-build signed-host names. Rationale: The ~del.vbs.bat filename and the _CL_###### folder naming are called out verbatim by Group-IB as durable, build-independent artifacts; they carry almost no legitimate collision and survive the per-build rotation of signed hosts/DLLs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-nexus-jadeprox-uses-new-triback.html • https://cyberpress.org/jadeprox-triback-campaign/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated installer that happens to name a temp folder _CL_<6 digits> (rare — the fixed 6-digit width narrows this)
  • A custom admin script literally named ~del.vbs.bat (effectively never seen in the wild)
  • Backup software re-creating a previously captured folder tree containing these artifacts
  • Malware-analysis sandbox replaying the sample on a monitored host
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the parent folder of the artifact — expect the side-load triad (signed EXE + DLL + .dat/.log) nearby; capture the ~del.vbs.bat contents for the cleanup targets it references. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the _CL_ folder for forensics before the batch self-deletes it. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1/UC2 hits on the same host and sweep peers for identical artifact names to scope the intrusion.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "~del.vbs.bat"
    or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\_CL_[0-9]{6}\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "~del.vbs.bat"
    or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)\\_CL_[0-9]{6}\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

JadeProx C2 / staging egress: claude-pro[.]com set and 43.106.71[.]28:8000 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoints reaching JadeProx command-and-control and staging infrastructure — the Beagle/AdaptixC2 domains (license.claude-pro[.]com, gouvvbo[.]top, security-vendor lookalikes) and the Alibaba Cloud staging host 43.106.71[.]28 on port 8000. Covers both the malvertising download of the fake Claude installer and post-install beaconing. Rationale: Every domain/IP here is dual-sourced: Group-IB's blocklist and Sophos both list claude-pro.com, license.claude-pro.com (8.217.190.58), gouvvbo.top, vertextrust-advisors.com and the update-<vendor>.com trio; THN adds the 43.106.71.28:8000 staging host. Direct-IOC network match is high-fidelity for a China-nexus targeted operation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/donuts-and-beagles-fake-claude-site-spreads-backdoor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-claude-ai-website-delivers-new-beagle-windows-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox appliance actively detonating the sample and reaching the C2 (whitelist the analysis host)
  • A security researcher browsing claude-pro.com from a corporate device for investigation
  • Passive DNS/IOC-scanner tooling that resolves the domains without a real infection
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse — 209.189.190.206 is a Cloudflare origin and could later front benign sites (validate the SNI/host header)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in ("43.106.71.28","8.217.190.58","178.128.108.89","192.252.186.62")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a signed vendor EXE from AppData/Startup or msiexec confirms the chain; note whether traffic hit 43.106.71.28:8000 (staging) vs a Beagle C2 domain. 2) Contain: block all listed domains/IPs at the proxy/firewall and isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: pivot the host back to UC1–UC3 artifacts, and query the wider fleet for any resolution of claude-pro.com to catch malvertising victims who downloaded the fake Claude installer.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("claude-pro.com","sylverixstrategy.com","gouvvbo.top","vertextrust-advisors.com","update-trellix.com","update-crowdstrike.com","update-sentinelone.com")
    or RemoteIP in ("43.106.71.28","8.217.190.58","209.189.190.206","178.128.108.89","192.252.186.62")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("43.106.71.28","8.217.190.58","209.189.190.206","178.128.108.89","192.252.186.62")

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

            - '\Cookies'

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-11511", "CVE-2021-24139", "CVE-2021-31755", "CVE-2021-32305")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental

    object payload signature.

logsource:
    category: process_creation

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:

            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or SHA1 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or MD5 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or SHA1 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620") or MD5 in~ ("e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e6d66d192a779f195426db94d2568c03a9bd0d2e8f1972aa32a0317940ae19c2", "46dea8c1af85134a7b15fc7168386eadd15474b1a6159567b24e83d8a30fc6ef", "6c657caecbf3b27d16ff648537e17dfe67dd69ed07e029dc5b74b8b53625bee3", "586f27257d3eaee7d4bec9e9207c317a9caeded95eca3969739d7e8181d24620"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hosts exposed to RefluXFS XFS reflink LPE (CVE-2026-64600) AIExploitation High
Surfaces RHEL/Fedora/Amazon Linux/Oracle/Rocky/Alma hosts still running an unpatched kernel vulnerable to CVE-2026-64600, so multi-tenant and shell-accessible hosts can be prioritised for the backported kernel + reboot. Article-specific because it pins the exact CVE Qualys disclosed and the distro families that ship reflink-enabled XFS by default. Rationale: Anchored on the exact CVE-2026-64600 identifier and the distro families (RHEL/Fedora Server/Amazon Linux/Oracle/Rocky/Alma/CloudLinux) named in the article and confirmed by the Qualys blog; a pure exposure hunt with near-zero FP because it keys on a scanner-asserted CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/new-refluxfs-linux-flaw-lets-attackers-gain-root-privileges/ • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/22/14
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched per RHSA-2026:39179/39180/39494 but scanner cache is stale (kernel installed, not yet rebooted — TVM reports the running kernel, so this is actually a true positive worth chasing)
  • Non-XFS or reflink=0 root filesystem where the scanner keys on kernel version alone and over-reports exposure
  • RHEL 7 hosts flagged by version heuristics despite predating XFS reflink support
  • EUS/SAP streams where the fixed erratum landed on a different date and the KB mapping lags
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host truly meets the exploit conditions — run `xfs_info / | grep reflink=` (and on other mounted XFS volumes); reflink=1 plus a running pre-fix kernel = exposed. Check `uname -r` against the relevant RHSA fixed version. 2) Contain: schedule/apply the vendor kernel erratum and REBOOT (package install alone does not replace the running kernel); prioritise multi-tenant, CI, and shell-accessible hosts. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, pivot to UC2/UC3 to look for reflink-clone activity against /etc/passwd or setuid binaries and post-exploit root escalation during the exposure window.

Unprivileged reflink clone of /etc/passwd or setuid-root binary (RefluXFS primitive) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the first step of the RefluXFS chain — a non-root user reflink-cloning a root-owned sensitive file it only has read access to (the article: 'clones a root-owned file into a scratch file with FICLONE'). Targets the accessible `cp --reflink` tooling variant against /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and common setuid-root binaries the PoC modifies to gain root. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit primitive (reflink-clone of a root-owned file the attacker only reads) plus the confirmed targets /etc/passwd and setuid-root binaries; the `--reflink` flag against those specific paths by a non-root user is an extremely rare legitimate operation. Custom compiled FICLONE exploits evade the cmdline anchor, so pair with UC1 exposure and UC3 payoff. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/refluxfs-linux-kernel-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/restore tooling using `cp --reflink=auto` over /etc during config staging (usually runs as root — excluded by the non-root filter)
  • Ansible/config-management modules that copy /etc/passwd templates with reflink=auto under a service account
  • Developer testing XFS reflink behaviour with cp --reflink on scratch copies of system files
  • Container image build steps that reflink-copy /etc during layer assembly on an XFS overlay
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","python3","cfagent","puppet","salt-minion") or InitiatingProcessAccountName == "root"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line, the invoking user, and the scratch destination path; confirm the source is a genuinely root-owned sensitive file and the user is unprivileged (no sudo entitlement). Check whether the host is unpatched (UC1). 2) Contain: suspend the account's shell/CI access on that host and snapshot /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and the referenced setuid binaries for integrity comparison against a known-good/package baseline (rpm -V). 3) Hunt: on the same host+user, look within the following minutes for `chsh`/`chfn` execution and any successful root escalation (UC3), plus repeated O_DIRECT write activity from the same process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--reflink"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/usr/bin/passwd","/usr/bin/sudo","/usr/bin/chsh","/usr/bin/chfn","/bin/su","/usr/bin/su","/usr/bin/mount","/usr/bin/pkexec")
| where isnotempty(AccountName) and AccountName != "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--reflink"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/usr/bin/passwd","/usr/bin/sudo","/usr/bin/chsh","/usr/bin/chfn","/bin/su","/usr/bin/su","/usr/bin/mount","/usr/bin/pkexec")
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername != "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RefluXFS reset primitive (chsh/chfn) followed by passwordless root escalation AIInstallation Medium
Correlates the article's named reset trick — an unprivileged user running `chsh` to reset the block's unshared state — with a subsequent switch to root on the same host within a short window, capturing the RefluXFS payoff where the attacker strips the root password in /etc/passwd and then logs in / su's to root. Article-specific because chsh is explicitly called out as the condition-reset step and /etc/passwd/root are the demonstrated target. Rationale: chsh is the exact reset primitive the article names ('an unprivileged user can reset that condition by running chsh'), and passwordless root via a modified /etc/passwd is the demonstrated payoff; correlating a non-root chsh with root escalation on the same host inside 10 minutes is far higher fidelity than either signal alone. Datadog/Falcon queries surface the chsh reset primitive (correlation applied at rule level, since those bare queries can't express the temporal join). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-old-refluxfs-linux-flaw-gives.html • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin legitimately changing their login shell with chsh, then running sudo for normal admin work within 10 minutes
  • New-user onboarding scripts that set the shell (chsh) and then a privileged account provisions the box
  • Interactive troubleshooting where an engineer flips shells and escalates during the same session
  • Config-management run that adjusts a service account shell then executes root-context tasks (filter by known automation parent processes)
Suppression filter
| where ViaAccount != ResetUser and isnotempty(ResetUser)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reset user is genuinely unprivileged (no legitimate sudo/root entitlement) and inspect whether root's password field in /etc/passwd is empty or recently altered while mtime looks stale — the RefluXFS write bypasses the inode, so content-hash the file against a package/backup baseline rather than trusting mtime. Check host is unpatched (UC1). 2) Contain: lock the root account / rotate the root password, kill the suspicious root session, and isolate the host if the passwd baseline shows out-of-band modification. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 for the reflink-clone that preceded this, review any setuid binaries modified out-of-band (rpm -V), and check for lateral SSH from this host using newly minted root credentials.
let win = 10m;
let ResetPrimitive = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("chsh","chfn")
    | where isnotempty(AccountName) and AccountName != "root"
    | project ResetTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ResetUser = AccountName, ResetCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName == "root"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("su","sudo","login","sshd","bash","sh")
| join kind=inner ResetPrimitive on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + win)
| project ResetTime, RootTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, ResetUser, ResetCmd, RootProcess = FileName, RootCmd = ProcessCommandLine, ViaProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ViaAccount = InitiatingProcessAccountName, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ResetTime)
| order by RootTime desc
let win = 10m;
let ResetPrimitive = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("chsh","chfn")
    | where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername != "root"
    | project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ResetUser = ActorUsername, ResetCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername == "root"
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("su","sudo","login","sshd","bash","sh")
| join kind=inner ResetPrimitive on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + win)
| project ResetTime, RootTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ResetUser, ResetCmd, RootProcess = ActingProcessName, RootCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ViaProcess = ParentProcessName, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ResetTime)
| order by RootTime desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:chsh OR @process.name:chfn) -@user.id:0 -@user.name:root
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 event_platform=Lin ImageFileName=/\/(chsh|chfn)$/i
| UserName!=root
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

logsource:
    category: process_creation

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

references:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows

    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

Attackers Weaponize GitHub Actions Runners to Target cPanel and WHM Servers

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 17 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a large-scale campaign that has turned compromised GitHub repositories into distributed attack infrastructure designed to target cPanel and WebHost Manager (WHM) instances. The activity involves malicious Packagist development versions spanning 10 packages associated with a legitimate PHP and DevOps developer, dinushchathurya, between July 12 and 13,

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] cPanel/WHM CVE-2026-41940 auth-bypass exploitation on control-panel ports (2087/2083) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network beacon to cPanel-harvester C2 43.228.157.68 (payload pull + credential exfil) · [LLM] DNSHook C2 channel resolution (dnshook.site + campaign GUID f5b0b742-…) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Network beacon to cPanel-harvester C2 43.228.157.68 (payload pull + credential exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host in the estate contacting the campaign's hard-coded C2 at 43.228.157.68, which serves the architecture-specific Linux scanning/exploitation payload and receives HTTP POST uploads of harvested AWS/GitHub/GitLab/Stripe/SSH secrets. Article-specific because the IP is the single fixed infrastructure node across all 583 malicious workflows. Rationale: 43.228.157.68 is the single fixed C2 named in the article (payload download + POST exfil) and corroborated by Socket/Rapid7/Cyberpress write-ups; a literal-IP match is maximally high-fidelity with essentially no legitimate traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-41940-cpanel-whm-authentication-bypass/ • https://cyberpress.org/github-actions-cpanel-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating the sample in a sandbox that egresses through corporate network
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning platform actively probing the C2 IP
  • Shared-hosting NAT egress where an unrelated tenant reuses the same upstream address (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/user on the flagged host and whether the host is a CI runner, dev workstation, or internet-facing cPanel/WHM box; pull the full flow (bytes out suggests exfil vs. small pull suggests payload fetch). 2) Contain: block 43.228.157.68 at egress/firewall, isolate the host, and rotate any AWS/GitHub/GitLab/Stripe/SSH/SendGrid/Mailgun secrets that lived on it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId/aid for connections to dnshook.site and for the architecture-detection payload; check whether the host consumed any dinushchathurya Packagist dev versions or ran attacker GitHub Actions workflows.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.228.157.68"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "43.228.157.68"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

cPanel/WHM CVE-2026-41940 auth-bypass exploitation on control-panel ports (2087/2083) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts exploitation of the CVE-2026-41940 CRLF-injection authentication bypass against internet-facing cPanel/WHM, which the campaign's payload uses to seize root on the control panel. Targets requests to the WHM/cPanel login/session endpoints on ports 2087/2083/2086/2082 carrying manipulated whostmgrsession cookies — the exact primitive documented by watchTowr/Rapid7. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated CVE-2026-41940 mechanics (whostmgrsession cookie manipulation on WHM 2087 / cPanel 2083, watchTowr/Rapid7) rather than a generic web-scan template; the cookie-name + control-panel-port pair is far more specific than plain 'login page hit'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-41940-cpanel-whm-authentication-bypass/ • https://censys.com/advisory/cve-2026-41940/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/cve-2026-41940-explained-cpanel-whm-authentication-bypass-hit-1-5m-servers
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WHM administrators or reseller accounts logging in from automation on 2087/2083 with valid whostmgrsession cookies
  • Uptime/health-check monitors polling the WHM login page
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) authenticated-checking cPanel
  • Backup or migration tooling (e.g. WHM transfer) hitting session endpoints programmatically
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<your-monitoring-subnet-not-applicable>")  // instead: baseline known-admin source IPs; here we retain signal by requiring RequestMethod POST plus whostmgrsession which excludes simple GET health checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged WHM/cPanel host, correlate the request to /var/cpanel/... session files and check for a session assuming user=root without a preceding successful interactive login; confirm the server version is below 11.136.0.5 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: patch to 11.136.0.5+ immediately, terminate active WHM sessions, and rotate all reseller/root and downstream account credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for follow-on secret theft (SSH keys, .env, AWS/Stripe creds), check egress to 43.228.157.68 and dnshook.site, and review whether the attack arrived from GitHub-hosted runner egress ranges.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort in (2087, 2083, 2086, 2082)
| where RequestURL has_any ("login", "session", "cpsess")
| where RequestCookies has "whostmgrsession" or RequestContext has "whostmgrsession" or RequestMethod == "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestCookies, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

DNSHook C2 channel resolution (dnshook.site + campaign GUID f5b0b742-…) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution of the campaign's DNSHook out-of-band channel — the unique identifier f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d under dnshook.site appears across ~6,100 workflow files and is used to report execution status/exfil over DNS. The GUID makes this a near-zero-FP indicator tying a host to this specific operation. Rationale: The GUID f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d is a campaign-unique DNSHook identifier called out in the article and echoed across ~6,100 workflows; matching it (or any dnshook.site subdomain) is a high-fidelity C2/exfil tell distinct from any generic DNS-tunneling rule. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attackers-weaponize-github-actions.html • https://cyberpress.org/github-actions-cpanel-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red team or bug-bounty researchers using dnshook.site as an OOB interaction service for their own testing
  • A pentest tool baked into a golden image periodically resolving dnshook.site as a connectivity check
  • DNS resolver/threat-intel sandbox pre-resolving indicators from a feed
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) issuing the query and whether the subdomain carries the campaign GUID (confirmed-malicious) versus a generic dnshook.site lookup (possible OOB testing); capture the full queried label as it may encode exfil data. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.dnshook.site at DNS, isolate the host, and rotate secrets reachable from it. 3) Hunt: pivot the host to egress toward 43.228.157.68, look for the architecture-detection Linux payload and cPanel/WHM scanning, and check for consumption of the ten dinushchathurya Packagist dev versions or attacker-added GitHub Actions workflows.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "dnshook.site" or RemoteUrl has "f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has "dnshook.site" or DnsQuery has "f5b0b742-240a-4811-8a5b-b0ba6060685d"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
