title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41940")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-41940")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel

Cisco Talos
2026-07-23 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group uses new malware "msaRAT" that hijacks browsers. The malware doesn't communicate directly with C2 but connects through the browser. It enables arbitrary command execution while hiding the attacker's IP from victims via WebRTC over TURN.

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1486
Domainsis-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev
IPs172.86.126.18
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
—
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent · [LLM] msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP AIDelivery High
Hunts the Chaos ransomware pre-ransom delivery step where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP on port 443) into C:\programdata\. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact filename, ProgramData sink, and hardcoded C2 IP. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim curl command from the article (update_ms.msi, hardcoded 172.86.126.18, ProgramData sink) — the triple combination is essentially unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using curl to stage a genuine .msi in ProgramData for software deployment
  • Internal software-distribution tooling pulling installers over HTTP to a ProgramData staging folder
  • Security researcher / detection-lab replaying the sample
  • RMM agent using curl to fetch an update package into ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible.exe","chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "172.86.126.18")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the curl invocation targeted 172.86.126.18 or the literal update_ms.msi filename and that the destination is C:\programdata\; pull the parent process and user. 2. Contain: network-isolate the host, block 172.86.126.18 at the perimeter, and quarantine C:\programdata\update_ms.msi before it is executed by msiexec. 3. Hunt: pivot to msiexec execution of that MSI, headless Chrome/Edge launches with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound traffic to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT Delivery via curl Downloading Fake Windows Update MSI to ProgramData
id: 6c2f4b1a-9d3e-4a77-8f2b-11a2c9d4e5f0
description: Detects Chaos ransomware msaRAT delivery where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 into ProgramData
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1218.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'update_ms.msi'
      - '172.86.126.18'
  location:
    CommandLine|contains: 'programdata'
  condition: selection and location
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) (@CommandLine:*update_ms.msi* OR @CommandLine:*172.86.126.18*) @CommandLine:*programdata*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/curl\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(update_ms\.msi|172\.86\.126\.18)/i

msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action) AIInstallation High
Hunts the second delivery stage: msiexec.exe executing the Chaos-dropped update_ms.msi whose custom action CA_Run_EA2AEBC3 reflectively loads lib.dll (msaRAT) into memory. Article-specific via the exact MSI filename. Rationale: The MSI filename update_ms.msi is a verbatim article IOC; msiexec running it from ProgramData is the reflective-load launcher for lib.dll (msaRAT). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor MSI happening to be staged in ProgramData (broad hunting clause only)
  • Patch-management tool invoking msiexec against a ProgramData-cached installer
  • Detection-lab replay of the sample
  • Third-party updater masquerading its own installer in ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm msiexec ran update_ms.msi and inspect the MSI's Binary table / custom action (CA_Run_*) and file metadata spoofing Microsoft. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill any child processes, and capture memory before reboot to recover the in-memory lib.dll (msaRAT). 3. Hunt: look for the RUN export being invoked, headless browser launches with CDP flags, and workers.dev / Twilio TURN egress to confirm C2 establishment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and TargetProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's core 'living off the browser' behaviour — it launches Chrome or Edge in headless mode with the CDP remote-debugging port enabled to drive a covert WebRTC C2. Detects browsers started with --headless/--remote-debugging-port by a parent that is not a browser or explorer. Rationale: The article states msaRAT launches Chrome/Edge headless via CreateProcessW with the remote-debugging port enabled to drive CDP; a browser started with these flags by a non-browser parent is a high-fidelity signal of programmatic browser hijack. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chaes-malware-now-uses-google-chrome-devtools-protocol-to-steal-data/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium automation frameworks launching headless Chrome for testing
  • CI/CD build agents rendering pages via headless Chrome
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services spawning headless browsers
  • Developer tooling that opens Chrome with --remote-debugging-port for debugging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe", "python.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cypress.exe", "chromedriver.exe", "selenium.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the parent process that spawned the headless browser and the remote-debugging port; benign automation parents (node.exe from a known project) differ sharply from msiexec/rundll32/unknown. 2. Contain: if the parent is unexpected, isolate the host and terminate the browser + parent process tree, then capture memory for the in-memory msaRAT. 3. Hunt: correlate with the CDP JSON endpoint (/json/list/) on localhost, WebRTC/TURN egress to global.turn.twilio.com, and connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects Chrome/Edge launched headless with CDP remote-debugging port by a non-browser parent, as used by Chaos ransomware msaRAT for covert browser-fronted C2
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i

msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network contact with the hardcoded Chaos/msaRAT infrastructure — the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev used for SDP/ICE exchange. Pure IOC pivot corroborated by Talos. Rationale: Both the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling domain are verbatim, campaign-unique IOCs from the Talos article; direct network matches are the highest-fidelity possible pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate host also using an unrelated *.workers.dev service (mitigated by the exact subdomain match)
  • Threat-intel sandbox / detonation VM deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security scanner probing the attacker IP
  • Proxy log replay from an IR investigation
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process (a browser process for the workers.dev signaling, or curl/msiexec for the delivery IP). 2. Contain: block 172.86.126.18 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev at the firewall/proxy and network-isolate the source host. 3. Hunt: on the host, look back for the curl download of update_ms.msi, msiexec execution, headless browser launch with CDP flags, RMM tooling, and outbound Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) traffic indicating the WebRTC DataChannel is live.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" or DestinationHostName =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New msaRAT malware uses Chrome, Edge browsers to route C2 traffic

BleepingComputer
2026-07-23 14 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware gang is using a new backdoor dubbed msaRAT that hides command-and-control (C2) communication by routing it through the Chrome or Edge browsers. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1566
Domainsis-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev
IPs172.86.126.18
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
—
Phase 2

Detected

Exploitation
Detected

Detected

Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] MSI masquerading as Windows Update (update_ms.msi) delivering msaRAT lib.dll · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New msaRAT malware uses Chrome, Edge browsers to route C2 traffic
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging by anomalous parent (msaRAT CDP C2 setup)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Browser contacting msaRAT Cloudflare Workers signaling host / staging IP · [LLM] Non-browser process connecting to localhost DevTools debug port (msaRAT loopback CDP control) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging by anomalous parent (msaRAT CDP C2 setup) AIInstallation High
Hunts msaRAT (lib.dll) launching a user-installed Chrome or Edge in headless mode with the remote-debugging interface enabled so it can drive the browser over Chrome DevTools Protocol. The combination of --headless plus --remote-debugging-port/-pipe spawned by a non-launcher parent is the browser-hijack initialization step that precedes all C2. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's execution primitive ('launches the browser in headless mode... enables the browser's remote debugging interface and connects to it via CDP'). --headless + --remote-debugging together, minus normal automation/launcher parents, is a rare, high-fidelity pair. Corroborated by Talos and The Hacker News write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1564.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium automation launched by node.exe or python.exe (excluded by parent filter but bespoke wrappers may slip through)
  • Synthetic web monitoring / uptime agents that headless-render pages
  • PDF-generation services (e.g. headless Chrome print-to-PDF) run by a backend service account
  • Security scanners / DAST tools that drive a headless browser
  • Internal RPA tooling that scripts a browser via CDP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\node_modules\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "playwright"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent lineage — confirm the parent is not a sanctioned automation host (node/python/CI agent) and capture the remote-debugging port value from the command line. Check whether an interactive user session exists on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the headless browser and its parent process tree, and block outbound to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and 172.86.126.18. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for update_ms.msi / lib.dll, a non-browser process connecting to 127.0.0.1 on the debug port, and subsequent traffic to *.workers.dev / Twilio TURN infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","userinit.exe","node.exe","python.exe","java.exe","electron.exe","code.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","msedgewebview2.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","userinit.exe","node.exe","python.exe","java.exe","electron.exe","code.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser contacting msaRAT Cloudflare Workers signaling host / staging IP AICommand & Control High
Alerts on any endpoint resolving or connecting to the msaRAT signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev or the staging IP 172.86.126.18. The browser fetches WebRTC connection info from this Cloudflare Worker to bootstrap the encrypted C2 channel, making the host a direct named IOC. Rationale: Uses the two confirmed network IOCs from Talos' IOC repo (the only published indicators): signaling host is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and staging IP 172.86.126.18. Both are unique, so any match is high-fidelity despite the workers.dev parent domain being shared with benign deployments. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app genuinely hosted on the same specific Worker subdomain (extremely unlikely given the random-looking name)
  • Threat-intel enrichment / sandbox detonation host deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Security researcher or IR analyst manually browsing to the IOC during investigation
  • Shared-egress NAT attributing the resolution to the wrong internal host (verify the true source via endpoint DNS)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the true source host and the process that initiated the resolution/connection (chrome.exe/msedge.exe expected). Confirm whether a headless browser with remote-debugging was launched on that host in the preceding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and 172.86.126.18 at DNS/proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same IOC, look for update_ms.msi / lib.dll and headless-browser launches, and pivot on outbound WebRTC/TURN traffic from browser processes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MSI masquerading as Windows Update (update_ms.msi) delivering msaRAT lib.dll AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the msaRAT delivery step where msiexec executes an installer named to look like a Windows update (update_ms.msi) that loads lib.dll into memory. Scopes to msiexec invocations with update-style MSI naming spawned outside legitimate patching channels (WU/SCCM/TrustedInstaller). Rationale: Anchors on the corroborated filename update_ms.msi (surfaced in Talos coverage / Help Net Security) and the article's statement that the MSI 'posing as a Windows update' loads lib.dll in memory. Parent exclusions strip legitimate WU/SCCM/TrustedInstaller patching to keep the update-style naming heuristic usable. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software updaters that name their MSI packages with 'update' or version/KB strings and run outside SCCM
  • Admin-driven manual patch installs from a network share or Downloads folder
  • Vendor agent self-update MSIs (e.g. driver/firmware update packages) launched by a helper service not in the exclusion list
  • Software packaging/test labs building MSIs named update*.msi
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\ccmcache\\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "\\SoftwareDistribution\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the referenced .msi and check signer — a Microsoft-signed, WU-catalogued update is benign; an unsigned/unknown signer named like an update is not. Review parent process and how the MSI reached the host (email attachment, RMM push, share). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the MSI and any dropped lib.dll, and terminate any headless browser processes. 3) Hunt: search for lib.dll image loads into non-standard hosts, headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging, and connections to the workers.dev signaling host across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has ".msi" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","KB","patch") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/i","/quiet","/qn"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","wuauclt.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","msiexec.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (ActingProcessCommandLine has ".msi" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","KB","patch"))
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("services.exe","ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","wuauclt.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MSI Masquerading as Windows Update - msaRAT update_ms.msi

Non-browser process connecting to localhost DevTools debug port (msaRAT loopback CDP control) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the msaRAT control channel where a non-browser process connects only to 127.0.0.1 to drive the headless browser over Chrome DevTools Protocol. Talos notes the implant 'talks to 127.0.0.1 and nothing else' — a non-browser initiator reaching the loopback DevTools port range is anomalous local-IPC-for-C2 behaviour. Rationale: Encodes Talos' distinguishing detail that the implant only ever talks to 127.0.0.1 and drives the browser over CDP. Scoping to the documented DevTools port range (9222-9299) with a non-browser initiator surfaces the loopback control channel; note the debug port is configurable, so pair with UC1 which reveals the actual port from the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or QA machines running Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium where the driver connects to the browser debug port (partially excluded by process filter)
  • IDE/editor debug integrations (VS Code, JetBrains) attaching to a Chromium debug port
  • Electron apps or embedded-browser tooling using CDP locally
  • Web performance/lighthouse tooling connecting to a local headless browser
  • Loopback IPC on 9222-9299 by unrelated apps that happen to use those ports
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\node_modules\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","lighthouse","selenium")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process image and command line — confirm it is not a sanctioned dev/automation tool, and check whether a headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging was launched on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the initiating process and the headless browser tree, and block the workers.dev signaling host and staging IP. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (headless launch) and UC2 (workers.dev egress) on the same DeviceId, and search for update_ms.msi / lib.dll to confirm the full msaRAT chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemotePort between (9222 .. 9299)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","node.exe","code.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemotePort between (9222 .. 9299)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","node.exe","code.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.

    - attack.execution

            - '\powershell.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Check Point Patches Exploited SmartConsole Flaw Allowing Full Admin Access

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-23 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Check Point has released security updates to address multiple vulnerabilities impacting Security Management and Multi-Domain Management (MDSM) products, including a critical flaw that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-16232 (CVSS score: 9.3), is an authentication bypass affecting the Check Point SmartConsole login process that allows an

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Check Point Mgmt Server contact with CVE-2026-16232 exploitation IPs · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Check Point Management admin auth/policy change from external or attacker source · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Check Point Mgmt Server contact with CVE-2026-16232 exploitation IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts network communication to/from the six attacker IPs Check Point published for the in-the-wild CVE-2026-16232/CVE-2026-62144 SmartConsole authentication-bypass campaign. Fires when an internet-exposed Security Management / MDSM server (or any internal host) talks to this confirmed exploitation infrastructure. Rationale: Anchored on the six exploitation IPs Check Point published in advisory sk185169 for the actively-exploited CVE-2026-16232 campaign; these are dedicated attacker infra so any contact is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Rapid7, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and the Check Point SKs which confirm the campaign and CISA-KEV listing. Cross-checked against: • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185169/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-16232-critical-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-exploited-in-the-wild/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-patches-smartconsole-zero-day-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/check-point-vulnerability-cve-2026-16232/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement sourcing from one of these IPs (unlikely — these are attacker-controlled)
  • Internal malware sandbox or TI-detonation host beaconing to the IP during analysis
  • SOC analyst manually connecting to the IOC IP during investigation
  • Recycled cloud/hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service (validate WHOIS/first-seen before closing)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandboxagent.exe","threatgrid.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm connection direction and the local asset — an inbound hit against the Security Management / MDSM server on the SmartConsole port is a probable CVE-2026-16232 exploitation attempt; note the source IP and timestamp. 2) Contain: block all six IPs at the perimeter, restrict Trusted Clients to trusted subnets, put the Management interface behind firewall, and apply the July 22 Jumbo hotfix; rotate all administrator credentials/API keys. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 — look for admin logins and policy/config changes from external sources and for run-script/exec-command activity on gateways in the same window.

Check Point Management admin auth/policy change from external or attacker source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SmartConsole/Management administrator authentication and security-policy actions originating from external (non-RFC1918) source IPs or from the campaign's IOC IPs. Targets the exact vulnerable condition Check Point described — Management exposed to the internet without Trusted-Client restrictions — where CVE-2026-16232 yields full-admin access. Rationale: Uses the article's stated vulnerable configuration ('Management exposed directly to the internet without IP restrictions') plus the six IOC IPs to surface admin authentication and policy actions from untrusted sources — the exploitation outcome (full admin, modify security policy) of CVE-2026-16232. Corroborated by Check Point sk185169 and Rapid7. Cross-checked against: • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185169/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-16232-critical-check-point-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-exploited-in-the-wild/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195848/hacking/check-point-patches-actively-exploited-smartconsole-authentication-bypass-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1078 T1548 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator managing Check Point remotely over an internet-exposed Management interface (the very config that should be remediated)
  • MSSP/managed-services provider connecting from an external but authorized source IP
  • Site-to-site VPN or NAT presenting an admin session with a public-looking source address
  • Automation/CI service account performing scheduled policy installs from a cloud egress IP
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known_admin_jump_host_public_ip_left_to_operator_allowlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the SourceIP against the admin allowlist and the six IOCs; an admin login or 'Install Policy'/'Publish' from an unrecognized external IP after a UC1 hit is high-confidence exploitation. 2) Contain: disable/rotate the affected admin account, restrict Trusted Clients to trusted subnets, place Management behind the firewall, and apply the July 22 Jumbo hotfix. 3) Hunt: enumerate every policy/rule change, new admin object, and gateway command executed in that session; roll back unauthorized changes and pivot to UC3.
let iocs = dynamic(["151.241.99.207","151.241.99.233","158.62.198.182","192.142.10.99","139.28.37.250","194.213.18.137"]);
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor == "Check Point"
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("SmartConsole","Management","MDS","Multi-Domain","Security Management","Audit")
    or Activity has_any ("Login","Administrator Login","Policy Installation","Install Policy","Publish","Session")
| where SourceIP in (iocs) or not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
